transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. I... well, I'm here because I just can't seem to make my brain stop. I keep getting these absolutely awful, unwanted thoughts that just play on a continuous loop, telling me that I’ve missed something critical. And I don't just mean a small, everyday mistake, I mean something that's going to ruin everything. 

I work with numbers and data all day, so I'll be sitting there, and suddenly this thought hits me out of nowhere that I left a wrong number in a data release. And if I did that, the whole project could be compromised, the analysis would be ruined, it would be a complete disaster. But it's not just at work, it bleeds into my personal life, too. I'll be driving or trying to sleep and I'll suddenly start panicking about an unlocked back door, or I'll be terrified that a bill got paid from the wrong account and now my mortgage is going to bounce and I'll lose the house. 

And the worst part—the absolute worst part of all of this—is that I know I checked it. I know I did. I can literally picture myself verifying the spreadsheet cells or physically turning the deadbolt on the door, but my mind just... it won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused a disaster anyway. It's like my own memory isn't good enough for my brain, and it just keeps whispering, 'But what if you're wrong? What if you missed it?' It's completely exhausting, it takes up hours of my day just worrying about it, and I just can't live like this anymore.
Do you find yourself performing specific actions or rituals to try and calm down or make these thoughts go away?

Yes, yes exactly. I mean, I have to do something, right? Because the panic just builds and builds in my chest until I feel like I can't even breathe. So, to try and calm myself down and make that awful feeling stop, I end up... well, I end up going back and checking. But it's not a normal check. 

Like with my work, I will literally reopen the spreadsheets. I'll have already saved them, closed the program, maybe even started shutting down my computer, but the thought hits and I have to open them back up. And emails—if I'm sending out a data summary, I will go into my sent folder and I will reread those emails line by line, word for word, just staring at the screen to make absolutely sure there isn't a typo that's going to compromise the entire project. 

And it has to be done a certain way, too, which just makes it so much worse. It’s not just a quick glance to reassure myself. Whether it’s the spreadsheets at work, or checking the locks on the doors at home, or pulling up payment confirmations for my bills... I have to check them over and over in a very specific, set order. Like with the doors, it’s the front door deadbolt, then the back door, then the garage, and I have to jiggle the handle. If I mess up the order, or if the phone rings and interrupts me, or if my brain just doesn't get that... that specific 'click' where it finally feels safe, then none of it counts. I have to start the whole sequence over from the very beginning until it feels right. Until it feels safe.

It just takes over everything. I mean, I'll sit down at my computer to finalize a simple data batch that should take maybe thirty minutes, and because I have to keep reopening the files and rereading every single line and checking the confirmations in my exact order... I'll look at the clock and it’s pitch black outside. Some nights I’m still sitting at my desk hours and hours later, just completely drained, and the most frustrating part of it all is that with all that time spent, nothing is actually finished. I'm just trapped doing the same things over and over again.
Have these thoughts and rituals interfered with your relationships or daily activities outside of work?

Oh, God, yes. Completely. It’s just... it’s ruined everything. It really has. I mean, I know I just mentioned staying late at my desk, but it’s not just that I’m working long hours—it’s that I’m actually falling behind on major, major work deadlines. And in my field, you know, doing data modeling and statistical analysis, deadlines are everything. The project managers are waiting on my numbers to move forward with their reports, and I’m just... I’m sitting there at 8 PM, 9 PM, reviewing the same spreadsheet for the fiftieth time, and I still don't actually finish it. I just can't bring myself to hit 'send' because the fear is so loud. So my performance is completely tanking, and my boss is starting to ask questions, which just adds to the panic.

And outside of work... well, I used to have a life. I really did. I used to be so active. I had this great group of friends and we would do salsa nights every Thursday. It was wonderful, you know, the music, the dancing, just getting out of my head and moving. I even bought these beautiful dancing shoes with the suede soles, and we'd go to this little club downtown. But... I've completely stopped going. I haven't been in months. Because by the time Thursday evening rolls around, I'm either still trapped at the office doing my checking rituals, or I finally get home and then I get stuck checking the doors and the bank accounts, and before I know it, it's 9:30 or 10:00 at night and I've missed the whole thing. I can't get away from the reviewing in time to actually meet them.

And it's the exact same story with my weekends. I love being out on the water. I have this beautiful sea kayak, a bright yellow one, and I used to take it out on the river every Saturday morning. It was so peaceful. Just the paddle and the water, the birds... it was my reset for the week. But you can't just go kayaking, right? You have to pack the gear, secure it to the roof rack, make sure the house is locked up before you leave... and that's where it all falls apart for me now. 

I'll get the kayak up on the car, tie it down, and then I'll go to lock the front door, and then the sequence starts. The deadbolt, the back door, the garage. And if I don't get that specific 'safe' feeling, I have to start over. I have literally stood in my driveway for two hours on a Saturday morning, just going back and forth, checking the straps on the kayak, checking the locks on the house, checking the straps again, checking the locks again, until I'm just so exhausted and crying in the driveway that I just take the kayak down, put it back in the garage, and go inside. I just give up. So, yes, it's interfering. I don't dance anymore. I don't paddle anymore. I just... I just check things. That's my whole life now.
Do you feel like these checking rituals are necessary to prevent something bad from happening?

I... gosh, I don't really know. I don't know if I actually think they're necessary to *prevent* it. It's... it's so hard to explain, because if you ask me logically, I know exactly how ridiculous it sounds. I mean, I’m 53 years old, I’m a completely rational person in every other aspect of my life. I work in mathematical sciences, you know? I deal with concrete data, statistical probabilities, hard facts all day long. So the rational part of my brain—the part that analyzes numbers for a living—knows perfectly well that reopening a saved spreadsheet for the fifth time isn't going to literally alter reality. It's not going to magically rewrite a wrong number if I already typed it. 

And the doors at home... I don't actually think that jiggling the garage door handle in my exact, specific sequence is what physically keeps a burglar out. A locked door is a locked door, right? The deadbolt doesn't care what order I check it in. So, I can't really say I believe the checking itself prevents the disaster. It’s not like I think I have some sort of supernatural power to stop the universe from falling apart just by staring at my sent emails or standing in my driveway for two hours. 

But... I just don't know. Because even though I know it doesn't make logical sense, the feeling in my chest just completely takes over. It's this overwhelming, crushing dread. It’s like my brain tells me that if I don't do the checking, and then the disaster *does* happen, it will be entirely my fault because I didn't do the one thing my mind was screaming at me to do. Like if I just walk away from the kayak and the car, and I ignore the urge to do the lock sequence, and then someone actually does break into the house... I'd never be able to forgive myself. Not because my little sequence would have physically stopped a break-in, but because I ignored the warning, if that makes any sense at all? 

So I honestly couldn't tell you if I think it actually prevents anything. I really don't know what I think it does. I just know that the panic gets so loud, and the 'what ifs' get so incredibly aggressive, that I literally cannot function until I give in to it. I just... I don't have any other way to make that awful, tight feeling in my chest go away.
Do you feel like you have any control over when these unwanted thoughts start?

Control? Oh, no. No, absolutely none. Zero. If I had any control over when they start, I... well, I wouldn't be sitting here right now, to be completely honest with you. That’s actually the entire reason I finally came in to see someone. I just... I keep getting these awful, completely unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical, and they just hit me out of absolutely nowhere. I could be driving to the grocery store, or just making my morning coffee, feeling completely fine, and suddenly it's like a lightning bolt hits my brain and ruins everything.

It will just scream at me that I put a wrong number in a major data release for work. Or that I left the back door unlocked when I left the house and now anyone can just walk right in. Or even something as stupid as paying a utility bill—my brain will convince me that I got a bill paid from the wrong account, and now my mortgage payment is going to bounce and I'll lose the house. And it’s so incredibly frustrating, doctor, because I *know* I checked. I know I did! I can literally see myself doing it in my memory. But my mind just grabs onto that tiny, microscopic sliver of doubt and it absolutely won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused a massive disaster. 

I try to push them away, I really do. I try to use my analytical skills, you know? I try to use logic. I tell myself that I looked at the spreadsheet, I locked the door, I checked the routing number on the bill. But it doesn't matter what the logical part of my brain says. The thoughts just completely hijack my mind. They just loop and loop and loop, getting louder and more terrifying, telling me that the data is ruined and I'm going to be fired, or someone is hiding in my house, or my finances are ruined. So no, I don't have any control over them starting. They just barge in and take over, and no matter how much I try to rationalize with myself, no matter how many times I know I already checked the thing, my mind just completely refuses to let go of the idea that a disaster is happening and it's entirely my fault. It's just exhausting. It really, really is.
Do you feel like performing these checking rituals helps reduce the anxiety caused by these unwanted thoughts?

Well... yes. Temporarily, anyway. I mean, that's really the only reason I do it. When that awful, tight feeling hits and my mind is screaming at me that I've ruined something, the only way I can calm myself down is to just give in to it. 

I end up reopening those spreadsheets—and not just glancing at them, I mean I am staring at them, tracing the cells with my finger. Or with my messages, I'll sit there rereading emails line by line, checking every single word, every attachment, every person copied on the thread, just to make absolutely sure I didn't send the wrong data to the wrong person. And it's the exact same thing with the locks on the house, or those payment confirmations for the utility bills I was telling you about. I have to check them over and over again, and it has to be in this very specific, set order. If I get interrupted, or if I lose count, or if I just don't get that right feeling, the panic flares right back up and I have to start the whole sequence over from the very beginning. 

I just have to keep doing it until it finally feels... 'safe.' Until my brain finally gives me permission to stop and the dread lifts just a tiny bit. But getting to that 'safe' feeling takes so much time, doctor. It takes so incredibly long. Like I said, some nights I’m still sitting there at my desk hours later, the whole office building is completely dark, the cleaning crew has already vacuumed around my cubicle and gone home, and I have absolutely nothing actually finished. I haven't produced a single piece of new work. I've just spent four hours trying to extinguish that anxiety by checking the same exact things over and over. So, yes, it does bring the anxiety down eventually, but it completely eats my life in the process.
Do you feel like these thoughts and rituals are affecting your ability to enjoy or participate in activities you once found pleasurable?

Oh, completely. It’s... gosh, it’s actually ruining everything I used to love. Everything. 

I mean, I know I mentioned earlier about staying late at the office, but the reality of that is so much worse than just working long hours. I’m actually falling behind on major work deadlines now. Major, critical deadlines. Because I’ll sit there, and I’ll stay late reviewing the same data sets, the same statistical models, over and over and over again, but I still don’t actually *finish* anything. The time just evaporates while I'm stuck in that loop, and the actual work doesn't get submitted. 

And as for my personal life, or things I do for fun... it’s just devastating, doctor. I used to have a real life outside of work. I used to go to these salsa nights downtown. Every Thursday, a group of us would go, and it was so wonderful, you know? Just the music, the movement, getting to turn off all that analytical, heavy math-brain stuff for a few hours and just be present. But I’ve completely stopped going. I had to drop out entirely. Because salsa starts at 7:30, and I’d tell myself, 'Okay, I’m going to leave the office right at 6:00.' But then 6:00 comes, and I have to check the email I just sent. And then it's 6:45, and I'm still checking it. Or if I actually manage to make it home to change clothes, I get stuck doing the lock sequence on the doors, and suddenly it's 8:15, and I’ve missed the whole class, and I'm just sitting in my hallway feeling completely defeated. I just can't get away from the checking and reviewing in time to actually make it anywhere.

It’s the exact same story with my kayaking. I love kayaking. Getting out on the water, the quiet, the nature... it used to be my sanctuary on the weekends. But getting the kayak loaded, strapping it to the car, making sure the house is secure before I drive out to the lake... the checking just spirals completely out of control. I'll check the straps, then the locks, then the straps again, and I literally can’t get away from the house in time to make the trip worth it. The whole morning just vanishes while I'm standing in my driveway. So I just... I just don't do it anymore. I haven't taken the kayak down in months. My whole world has just shrunk down to my desk and my front door, basically. It’s taken all the joy out of everything, because I know even if I try to plan something fun, the rituals are just going to steal the time away anyway.
Do you feel like you are compelled to perform these rituals to neutralize the anxiety caused by your unwanted thoughts?

Yes, exactly. Compelled is... well, it's the perfect word for it, really. I know I was just rambling about this a minute ago, but it truly isn't a choice. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, 'Oh, I should probably double-check my work just to be thorough.' It's this overwhelming, crushing dread, like a physical weight on my chest, and to calm myself down, to just neutralize that horrible feeling, I absolutely *have* to do the routines. 

I just... I end up reopening those spreadsheets, and I'm rereading emails line by line, just scouring them, terrified I've made some catastrophic error. And it’s the exact same compulsion with checking the locks at home, or looking at those payment confirmations I mentioned. I have to check them over and over again, and it absolutely has to be in a very specific, set order. If I mess up the order—like if I check the deadbolt before the knob, or look at the routing number before the account number—it doesn't count. The anxiety just flares right back up, and I have to start the whole thing over. 

I have to keep going, repeating the whole sequence, until it finally feels 'safe.' Until my brain just... lets me off the hook for a second and gives me that tiny bit of relief. But the cost of getting to that 'safe' feeling is just enormous. Like I said before, it's why some nights I’m still at my desk hours later, the whole office building is dead quiet, the heating has turned off for the night, and I'm just sitting there completely exhausted with nothing actually finished. Not a single new calculation done, no new work produced. Just hours and hours stolen by trying to neutralize that panic so I can finally breathe.
Do you feel like these unwanted thoughts are intrusive and enter your mind against your will?

Oh, completely against my will. It’s not like I’m sitting there inviting them in or trying to brainstorm worst-case scenarios. They just... they ambush me. Honestly, that’s the entire reason I finally came in to get help, because I just keep getting these awful, completely unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical, and they just force their way into my head out of nowhere. 

I'll just be sitting there, maybe trying to eat lunch or drive home, and suddenly my brain will just scream at me that I’ve made some horrible mistake. Like with my work—working with data and statistics all day, accuracy is everything, right? So my mind will just flash this vivid, terrifying idea that I’ve put a wrong number in a major data release. Just one transposed digit or a decimal point in the wrong column, and I'll suddenly be picturing this massive, catastrophic chain reaction where the whole project collapses and people lose their jobs all because of me. 

And it’s the exact same thing with the house. I’ll be miles away, and this thought will just slam into my head that there’s an unlocked back door, and someone is going to break in and destroy everything. Or that a bill got paid from the wrong account—like those utility bills I keep mentioning—and that my electricity is going to get shut off, or my credit will be ruined. The thoughts just hijack my brain. 

And the absolute worst part, doctor... the thing that makes me feel like I'm losing my mind... is that even when I *know* I checked it. Even when I can literally picture myself staring at the account number, or I can feel the memory of turning the deadbolt on the back door... my mind just won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused a disaster. It just grips me. It tells me, well, maybe you unlocked it right after, or maybe you looked at the wrong row on the spreadsheet when you were verifying it. It just won't stop playing. It’s like a broken record playing at maximum volume, and I can't find the plug to pull it out of the wall. I just want some peace and quiet in my own head, but these thoughts just barge in whenever they want and take over my entire reality. I mean, you can imagine how exhausting that is, just constantly being bombarded by your own brain when you're just trying to live a normal... well, what used to be a normal life, anyway.
Do you feel like these unwanted thoughts are a part of yourself or do they feel like they are coming from outside of your own thoughts?

No, no, they are definitely my own thoughts. It’s not like... I don't know, it's not like I'm hearing voices or someone else is putting them in my head or anything like that. It’s definitely me. And honestly, doctor, I think that’s what makes this whole thing so incredibly exhausting. It’s my own brain turning against me. 

Like I was just saying a moment ago, the entire reason I finally came in to see you is because I just keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical. But it's my own voice in my head telling me these things. It's my own mind flashing that image of a wrong number in a data release, or picturing an unlocked back door, or obsessing over a bill paid from the wrong account. It’s all generated right up here, by me. 

I think because I work in a mathematical field, my brain is just so trained to look for errors, to analyze every single variable. But now it's like that analytical part of me has just gone completely rogue. It's feeding on itself. Because I *am* a logical person, usually! I know how to verify data. I know how a lock works. But then my own mind just hijacks that logic. I can literally be standing right there, and even when I *know* I checked it—even when I have the physical, tangible memory of verifying the numbers or turning the deadbolt—my mind just absolutely won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused a disaster. 

It’s like my brain is split in two, you know? There’s the rational part of me that knows everything is fine, and then there’s this other part of my own mind that is just screaming at me that I ruined everything and people are going to suffer because of my negligence. It’s a civil war in my own head. If it were coming from outside, maybe I could just ignore it, or walk away from it, or tell whoever was saying it to shut up. But you can't walk away from your own thoughts, can you? You’re just trapped with them. Every single minute of the day, I'm just arguing with myself, trying to convince my own brain that we didn't cause a catastrophe, and my brain just refuses to listen to reason. It just keeps throwing these horrible "what ifs" at me, and I just... I can't escape myself.
Do you feel like these unwanted thoughts are recurring and persistent, even when you try to distract yourself or focus on other things?

Oh, they never stop. Never. Distraction is basically impossible at this point. I know I probably sound like a broken record, constantly repeating myself about the exact same things, but that's really the whole reason I came in—because I just keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical, and they simply do not go away no matter what I do to try and block them out. 

I could be trying to watch a movie, or read a book, or even just trying to have a nice, normal conversation with a friend over coffee, and suddenly, out of nowhere... it's just there. I'll be trying to focus on the plot of a television show, really trying to immerse myself in it, and my brain will just completely overlay it with that panic about a wrong number in a data release. Or I'll be trying to listen to someone talk about their weekend, and all I can hear in my head is this loud, screaming thought about an unlocked back door, or a utility bill paid from the wrong account. It's like trying to watch two different channels on the TV at the exact same time, but the channel broadcasting my mistakes is turned up to maximum volume and I can't find the remote.

I try so, so hard to push them away. I really do. I try to tell myself, 'You're at a restaurant, just enjoy your meal, focus on the menu, you checked everything before you left.' But like I was saying just a few minutes ago, even when I *know* I checked it—even when I can sit there and summon the literal memory of doing it correctly—my mind just absolutely won't let go of the possibility that I've caused a disaster. It just clings to it like a parasite. 

I'll try to do a Sudoku puzzle, or listen to a podcast, or reorganize my kitchen cabinets—literally anything to just drown the thoughts out and occupy my hands and my mind. But the thoughts are so loud and so relentless. They just gnaw and gnaw at me. It's like a dripping faucet in the background of my life, except every single drop is a reminder that I might have ruined my career or put my home in danger. It just wears you down, doctor, it really, truly does. You try to look away, you try to focus your eyes on literally anything else in the world, but the thoughts just grab your face and force you to look right back at them. You just can't distract yourself from your own mind.
Do you feel like your unwanted thoughts and checking rituals are significantly interfering with your overall quality of life?

Significantly interfering? Oh, doctor, "interfering" doesn't even begin to cover it. It has completely dismantled my life. I mean, there is really no quality of life left to speak of at this point. 

Take my job, for instance. I mentioned earlier how critical accuracy is in my field, working with all that data and statistics. Well, because of all this, I’ve actually fallen terribly behind on my major work deadlines. It’s humiliating, honestly. I’ve always prided myself on being the reliable one, the efficient one. But lately... I just stay late at the office, hours and hours after everyone else has packed up and gone home, just reviewing and reviewing the same datasets. I'll check the columns, verify the decimal points, trace every single formula back to its origin. And the absolute worst part is that I stay all that extra time, sacrificing my evenings, and I *still* don’t finish the work! Because every time I think I'm finally done and ready to submit it, my brain screams that I missed a row, or that I transposed a number in the very first batch, and I just have to start the entire review process all over again. 

And it bleeds into my personal time, too. I used to have hobbies, things I actually looked forward to that got me out of my own head. I used to go to these wonderful salsa nights downtown on Thursdays—I've been doing that for years, and it was such a great way to socialize and just move. And on the weekends, if the weather was nice, I’d take my kayak out on the water. Just being out in nature, paddling along the river... it was so peaceful. But I’ve completely stopped going to salsa nights, and my kayak is just gathering dust in the garage right now. 

I haven't done either of those things in months because... well, because I just can’t get away from the checking and reviewing in time to actually go do them. I’ll get dressed for salsa, and then I'll get stuck at the back door, checking the deadbolt over and over, pulling on the handle, walking away, and then running back because I'm terrified I actually unlocked it the last time I touched it. Or I'll be trying to load up my kayak, and I'll have to run back inside to check my computer to make absolutely certain those utility bills were paid from the right account before I can leave the house. By the time I finally feel like I might be able to step out the door—if I ever even reach that point—the dance class is already over, or the sun is going down and it's too late to hit the water. It just eats up every spare second I have. I mean, how can you possibly have any quality of life when it takes you three hours just to walk out of your own house? You just... you just eventually give up trying to go anywhere at all.
Do you feel an overwhelming urge to repeat these checking rituals until you feel a sense of completion or relief?

Overwhelming... yes, overwhelming is exactly the right word for it. It’s this intense, almost physical pressure that just builds and builds in my chest, and the only way to... well, to calm myself down, to make that screaming in my head stop, is to just give in and do the checks. I have to do them. 

So I end up reopening the same spreadsheets I just saved and closed two minutes prior. And it’s not just a quick glance to reassure myself, oh no. I am rereading emails line by line, literally tracing my finger across the monitor to make sure I didn't type a wrong digit or attach the wrong dataset. And it's the exact same thing with the house and my finances. I find myself checking the locks on the doors, and then pulling up my bank app to check the payment confirmations over and over again. 

But the thing is, doctor, it’s not just doing it once or twice. I have to do it in a very specific, set order. If I check the back deadbolt, and then I check the front door, and then I look at the utility bill confirmation... if I mess up that sequence, or if a car drives by and breaks my concentration while I'm doing it, I have to start the entire routine completely over from scratch. I just keep repeating that exact same loop, over and over and over, desperately waiting for that tiny click in my brain until it finally feels 'safe.' 

I just want that relief. I just want to feel like it's done and I haven't ruined anything. But that feeling of safety is so incredibly elusive. It takes so long to get there. Like I was saying earlier about falling behind at my job... that's exactly why. Because I get stuck in these loops, trying to find that sense of completion, and some nights I’m still sitting there at my desk hours later, the whole office building is completely dark and empty around me, and I have absolutely nothing actually finished. I’ve just spent three hours reopening and rereading the exact same files, just chasing that feeling of safety that never seems to come.
Do you feel like these unwanted thoughts are obsessive and recurring, dominating your mind for most of the day?

Well, yes, absolutely. Like I mentioned when we first started talking today, that is quite literally the entire reason I came in to see you. I just keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical, and it really does take up my entire day, from the second I open my eyes in the morning until I finally manage to pass out from sheer exhaustion at night. 

It's just a constant, rolling loop of panic. It's always about a wrong number in a data release, or an unlocked back door, or a bill being paid from the wrong account. And the most frustrating part of it all—and I know I brought this up earlier, but it just drives me absolutely crazy to think about—is that even when I *know* for a fact that I checked it, my mind simply won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused some sort of catastrophic disaster. 

I can literally picture myself turning the deadbolt, you know? I can see the confirmation screen for the bill payment in my mind's eye, clear as day, but my brain just says, 'Are you sure? What if you turned the lock back the other way by accident? What if you looked at the wrong row on the spreadsheet?' It just dominates everything. I'll be sitting in traffic on my commute, and instead of listening to the radio or thinking about what to make for dinner like a normal person, I'm just completely consumed by this dread that I’ve ruined my company's statistical report or left my house wide open to intruders. It never gives me a single moment of peace, doctor, it really doesn't. It's just all day, every day, this constant heavy cloud hanging right over my head, and I just can't seem to get out from under it no matter how hard I try to reason with myself.
Do you feel like you have to repeat these checking rituals until you feel a sense of relief or completion?

I feel like... well, I know we actually just touched on this a few moments ago, doctor, but yes, absolutely. That search for relief is the entire driver behind all of it. I know I can ramble on and on, so maybe I didn't emphasize it enough before, but to calm myself down, I just have to keep doing it until my brain gives me the green light. 

Like I was explaining earlier, I end up reopening those exact same spreadsheets I just saved, and I'm rereading my emails line by line. I mean, literally tracing the sentences on my monitor. And it’s the exact same exhausting process at home with checking the locks and the payment confirmations over and over. I have to do it all in that very specific, set order, because if I don't follow the sequence perfectly, I don't get that sense of completion. I don't get to feel 'safe.' 

And chasing that elusive feeling of safety is exactly why I end up so trapped. It’s why, like I mentioned, some nights I’m still sitting at my desk hours and hours later. The whole building will be completely dark, the janitorial staff has already come and gone, and I’m just sitting there in the glow of my screen, completely drained, with absolutely nothing actually finished for the day. I just cannot stop the cycle until I finally feel that sense of relief, no matter how long it takes or how much of my life it eats up in the process.
Do you feel like your unwanted thoughts and checking rituals are making it difficult for you to maintain relationships with friends and family?

Oh, it’s… it’s honestly just ruining everything. My social life is practically non-existent at this point, and it breaks my heart because I used to be so active. I used to have this really wonderful group of friends, and we had our things, you know? Like Thursday nights, for years, we would go to these salsa nights downtown. I absolutely loved it—the music, getting to just let loose and move around after staring at numbers and monitors all week. But I haven’t been to a single salsa night in... gosh, it has to be at least six months. Because I just can't get away from the checking and reviewing in time. I'll tell them I'll be there by seven, but seven rolls around and I'm still trapped at my desk, tracing my finger over the same spreadsheet I've been looking at since four o'clock.

patient.answer:
No, no, they are definitely my own thoughts. It’s not like... I don't know, it's not like I'm hearing voices or someone else is putting them in my head or anything like that. It’s definitely me. And honestly, doctor, I think that’s what makes this whole thing so incredibly exhausting. It’s my own brain turning against me. 

Like I was just saying a moment ago, the entire reason I finally came in to see you is because I just keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical. But it's my own voice in my head telling me these things. It's my own mind flashing that image of a wrong number in a data release, or picturing an unlocked back door, or obsessing over a bill paid from the wrong account. It’s all generated right up here, by me. 

I think because I work in a mathematical field, my brain is just so trained to look for errors, to analyze every single variable. But now it's like that analytical part of me has just gone completely rogue. It's feeding on itself. Because I *am* a logical person, usually! I know how to verify data. I know how a lock works. But then my own mind just hijacks that logic. I can literally be standing right there, and even when I *know* I checked it—even when I have the physical, tangible memory of verifying the numbers or turning the deadbolt—my mind just absolutely won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused a disaster. 

It’s like my brain is split in two, you know? There’s the rational part of me that knows everything is fine, and then there’s this other part of my own mind that is just screaming at me that I ruined everything and people are going to suffer because of my negligence. It’s a civil war in my own head. If it were coming from outside, maybe I could just ignore it, or walk away from it, or tell whoever was saying it to shut up. But you can't walk away from your own thoughts, can you? You’re just trapped with them. Every single minute of the day, I'm just arguing with myself, trying to convince my own brain that we didn't cause a catastrophe, and my brain just refuses to listen to reason. It just keeps throwing these horrible "what ifs" at me, and I just... I can't escape myself.

Or I'll be trying to listen to someone talk about their weekend, and all I can hear in my head is this loud, screaming thought about an unlocked back door, or a utility bill paid from the wrong account. It's like trying to watch two different channels on the TV at the exact same time, but the channel broadcasting my mistakes is turned up to maximum volume and I can't find the remote.

I try so, so hard to push them away. I really do. I try to tell myself, 'You're at a restaurant, just enjoy your meal, focus on the menu, you checked everything before you left.' But like I was saying just a few minutes ago, even when I *know* I checked it—even when I can sit there and summon the literal memory of doing it correctly—my mind just absolutely won't let go of the possibility that I've caused a disaster. It just clings to it like a parasite. 

I'll try to do a Sudoku puzzle, or listen to a podcast, or reorganize my kitchen cabinets—literally anything to just drown the thoughts out and occupy my hands and my mind. But the thoughts are so loud and so relentless. They just gnaw and gnaw at me. It's like a dripping faucet in the background of my life, except every single drop is a reminder that I might have ruined my career or put my home in danger. It just wears you down, doctor, it really, truly does. You try to look away, you try to focus your eyes on literally anything else in the world, but the thoughts just grab your face and force you to look right back at them. Significantly interfering? Oh, doctor, "interfering" doesn't even begin to cover it. It has completely dismantled my life. I mean, there is really no quality of life left to speak of at this point. 

Take my job, for instance. I mentioned earlier how critical accuracy is in my field, working with all that data and statistics. Well, because of all this, I’ve actually fallen terribly behind on my major work deadlines. It’s humiliating, honestly. I’ve always prided myself on being the reliable one, the efficient one. But lately... I just stay late at the office, hours and hours after everyone else has packed up and gone home, just reviewing and reviewing the same datasets. I'll check the columns, verify the decimal points, trace every single formula back to its origin. And the absolute worst part is that I stay all that extra time, sacrificing my evenings, and I *still* don’t finish the work! Because every time I think I'm finally done and ready to submit it, my brain screams that I missed a row, or that I transposed a number in the very first batch, and I just have to start the entire review process all over again. 

And it bleeds into my personal time, too. I used to have hobbies, things I actually looked forward to that got me out of my own head. I used to go to these wonderful salsa nights downtown on Thursdays—I've been doing that for years, and it was such a great way to socialize and just move. And on the weekends, if the weather was nice, I’d take my kayak out on the water. Just being out in nature, paddling along the river... it was so peaceful. But I’ve completely stopped going to salsa nights, and my kayak is just gathering dust in the garage right now. 

I haven't done either of those things in months because... well, because I just can’t get away from the checking and reviewing in time to actually go do them. I’ll get dressed for salsa, and then I'll get stuck at the back door, checking the deadbolt over and over, pulling on the handle, walking away, and then running back because I'm terrified I actually unlocked it the last time I touched it. Or I'll be trying to load up my kayak, and I'll have to run back inside to check my computer to make absolutely certain those utility bills were paid from the right account before I can leave the house. By the time I finally feel like I might be able to step out the door—if I ever even reach that point—the dance class is already over, or the sun is going down and it's too late to hit the water. It just eats up every spare second I have. I mean, how can you possibly have any quality of life when it takes you three hours just to walk out of your own house? You just... you just eventually give up trying to go anywhere at all.

I have to do them. 

So I end up reopening the same spreadsheets I just saved and closed two minutes prior. And it’s not just a quick glance to reassure myself, oh no. I am rereading emails line by line, literally tracing my finger across the monitor to make sure I didn't type a wrong digit or attach the wrong dataset. And it's the exact same thing with the house and my finances. I find myself checking the locks on the doors, and then pulling up my bank app to check the payment confirmations over and over again. 

But the thing is, doctor, it’s not just doing it once or twice. I have to do it in a very specific, set order. If I check the back deadbolt, and then I check the front door, and then I look at the utility bill confirmation... if I mess up that sequence, or if a car drives by and breaks my concentration while I'm doing it, I have to start the entire routine completely over from scratch. I just keep repeating that exact same loop, over and over and over, desperately waiting for that tiny click in my brain until it finally feels 'safe.' 

I just want that relief. I just want to feel like it's done and I haven't ruined anything. But that feeling of safety is so incredibly elusive. It takes so long to get there. Like I was saying earlier about falling behind at my job... that's exactly why. Because I get stuck in these loops, trying to find that sense of completion, and some nights I’m still sitting there at my desk hours later, the whole office building is completely dark and empty around me, and I have absolutely nothing actually finished. I’ve just spent three hours reopening and rereading the exact same files, just chasing that feeling of safety that never seems to come.
